title: Testing One Kinase Outside the Cell
endLine: A purified kinase plus labelled ATP shows what it can phosphorylate directly.

scenes.tts: A phosphate just landed on a protein. Which enzyme put it there? Your genome holds five hundred and eighteen protein kinases, enzymes that attach phosphate to proteins. In a living cell, many work at once, so you cannot see who did it.
scenes.caption: A phosphate just landed on a protein. Which enzyme put it there? Your genome holds 518 protein kinases, enzymes that attach phosphate to proteins. In a living cell, many work at once, so you cannot see who did it.
scenes.visual: Schematic cross-section of a crowded living cell filling most of the frame. Dozens of gently drifting enzyme shapes surround one target protein as a bright phosphate dot snaps onto it. A crisp question mark rises over the crowd while a schematic counter displays 518 protein kinases. No molecular structures.

scenes.visual: The crowded cell fades back while one candidate kinase and the target protein glide smoothly into a clean glass reaction chamber on the left (schematic). The title Testing One Kinase Outside the Cell fades in at full contrast, holds briefly, and clears while the glass chamber remains in place.

scenes.tts: Isolate one suspect outside the cell. An in vitro kinase assay mixes purified kinase, a substrate, and A T P with a labelled end phosphate. The kinase moves that end, or gamma, phosphate onto serine, threonine, or tyrosine. Near p H seven the phosphate adds close to two negative charges.
scenes.caption: Isolate one suspect outside the cell. An in vitro kinase assay mixes purified kinase, a substrate, and ATP with a labelled end phosphate. The kinase moves that end, or gamma, phosphate onto serine, threonine, or tyrosine. Near pH 7 the phosphate adds close to two negative charges.
scenes.visual: Inside the glass reaction chamber on the left (schematic), a two-lobed kinase shape sits beside a target substrate bar and an ATP token made of three linked beads with the end bead lit as the gamma phosphate. As narrated, the kinase transfers the lit bead onto a site marked serine, threonine, or tyrosine on the substrate. A two-bead ADP token drifts away while a negative-charge glow pulses on the substrate. Slow drifting particles keep the fluid alive. No molecular structures.
scenes.narration: Isolate one suspect outside the cell. An in vitro kinase assay mixes purified kinase, a substrate, and ATP with a labelled end phosphate. The kinase moves that end, or gamma, phosphate onto serine, threonine, or tyrosine. Near pH 7 the phosphate adds close to two negative charges.

scenes.tts: Next, detect the transferred phosphate. Track its label directly on the substrate. Or use a phosphospecific antibody, which binds only when one site carries phosphate. To find unexpected sites, the enzyme trypsin cuts the protein into short pieces called peptides. Mass spectrometry weighs each one closely enough that one phosphate shows.

scenes.visual: The glass chamber stays on the left while a readout panel opens on the right (schematic). First, the lit phosphate label glows directly on a substrate band. Next, a Y-shaped phosphospecific antibody locks onto one phosphorylated site and darkens a blot band. Finally, schematic trypsin scissors snip the substrate into short peptide bars that move onto a mass spectrometry plot where one phosphorylated peptide shifts apart so one phosphate shows (schematic).

scenes.tts: Suppose a signal arrives, and your antibody band turns much darker. Does that prove more substrate molecules carry phosphate? Think of two other ways that band could darken.
scenes.caption: Suppose a signal arrives, and your antibody band turns much darker. Does that prove more substrate molecules carry phosphate? Think of two other ways that band could darken.
scenes.visual: The readout blot on the right enlarges beside the glass chamber (schematic). A faint substrate band shifts to a much darker band below a Signal arrow, while the question Does a darker band prove more phosphate? appears above at full contrast.
scenes.narration: Suppose a signal arrives, and your antibody band turns much darker. Does that prove more substrate molecules carry phosphate? Think of two other ways that band could darken.

scenes.visual: The darkened blot band and the question Does a darker band prove more phosphate? remain steadily on screen while a slow ambient progress bar glides beneath the question (schematic).

scenes.tts: First, the sample may hold more total protein, not more phosphate. Blot the same samples for whole protein too. Second, an antibody can bind the wrong protein, so run a control missing the protein or phosphate. With those checks, a purified kinase plus labelled A T P shows what it can phosphorylate directly.

scenes.visual: Two control panels slide in beside the darkened blot band (schematic). Below the first band, a whole-protein blot appears to compare total protein across lanes. Beside it, a control lane missing the protein or the phosphate stays blank, ruling out binding to the wrong protein. The guiding sentence A purified kinase shows what it can phosphorylate directly appears cleanly along the lower frame.

scenes.tts: Three limits remain. An antibody misses unsuspected sites and never shows what fraction of molecules carry phosphate. Sites predicted by tools like Scansite stay guesses until someone finds the phosphate. And a cell-free mix lacks phosphatases, and its kinase may mark targets it never reaches inside cells.

scenes.visual: The glass chamber dims slightly on the left as three schematic limit cards cycle smoothly in the readout panel on the right: an antibody binding one marked site while an unmarked site stays hidden beside an unknown-fraction gauge; a sequence bar labelled Scansite guess with an empty phosphate slot; and the purified kinase marking a substrate in the glass chamber while, inside a schematic cell outline, the same substrate sits apart from the kinase and a phosphatase stands by.

scenes.tts: The assay unlocked major discoveries. At the end of the 1970s, Cohen's lab at Vanderbilt University used membranes from A four thirty-one tumor cells. They are rich in receptors for the growth factor E G F. With Graham Carpenter doing much of the biochemistry, adding E G F sped phosphate onto protein. Hiroshi Ushiro then found it landed on tyrosine.
scenes.caption: The assay unlocked major discoveries. At the end of the 1970s, Cohen's lab at Vanderbilt University used membranes from A-431 tumor cells. They are rich in receptors for the growth factor EGF. With Graham Carpenter doing much of the biochemistry, adding EGF sped phosphate onto protein. Hiroshi Ushiro then found it landed on tyrosine.
scenes.visual: Inside the glass chamber on the left, a schematic strip of A-431 tumor-cell membranes (no living cells) replaces the lone kinase, tagged Vanderbilt University, end of the 1970s. An EGF ligand docks on a membrane receptor and lit phosphates transfer rapidly onto membrane protein. On the right readout panel, the target marker highlights tyrosine beside the names Cohen, Graham Carpenter, and Hiroshi Ushiro (schematic).

scenes.tts: In 1998, De Koninck and Schulman tested purified cam kinase two, which calcium switches on through the calcium-binding protein calmodulin. When two neighbouring subunits hold calmodulin, one can phosphorylate the other, so activity can persist after calcium falls. They showed that lasting activity depends on pulse frequency.
scenes.caption: In 1998, De Koninck and Schulman tested purified CaM kinase II, which calcium switches on through the calcium-binding protein calmodulin. When two neighbouring subunits hold calmodulin, one can phosphorylate the other, so activity can persist after calcium falls. They showed that lasting activity depends on pulse frequency.
scenes.visual: In the glass chamber on the left, a schematic ring of subunits labelled CaM kinase II replaces the membrane strip. Schematic calcium pulses flash slowly, then rapidly; during rapid pulses, neighbouring subunits hold calmodulin and pass bright phosphates to each other. On the right readout panel, a schematic activity curve stays elevated after rapid pulses, tagged De Koninck and Schulman, 1998.

scenes.tts: Around 1990, a drug for one kinase's A T P pocket was expected to jam dozens. That pocket looks alike across kinases. In Basel, a group including Juerg Zimmermann added one methyl group, removing activity against protein kinase C. It still blocked A B L, and the compound became imatinib. One purified kinase shows what it can do directly.
scenes.caption: Around 1990, a drug for one kinase's ATP pocket was expected to jam dozens. That pocket looks alike across kinases. In Basel, a group including Juerg Zimmermann added one methyl group, removing activity against protein kinase C. It still blocked ABL, and the compound became imatinib. One purified kinase shows what it can do directly.
scenes.visual: In the glass chamber on the left, a small schematic blocker settles into the kinase ATP pocket while a single added methyl tag shifts its shape. On the right readout panel, a schematic selectivity grid shows the blocker no longer inhibiting protein kinase C (its row stays active) while ABL's row is blocked, tagged Basel, Juerg Zimmermann, imatinib. The chamber and readout settle into one clean final frame.
